summary: The article provides a largely accurate and comprehensive overview of Diwali gift tax rules in India for 2026, aligning well with current income tax provisions regarding gift taxation, exemptions, and definitions of 'relative'.

claims.claim: Gifts, whether in cash, movable, or immovable property, are taxable under the Income Tax Act, 1961, if their value exceeds ₹50,000 in a financial year.
claims.note: Section 56(2)(x) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, specifies that gifts exceeding ₹50,000 in a financial year are taxable as "Income from Other Sources".

claims.claim: If the aggregate value of such gifts from non-relatives crosses ₹50,000 in a financial year, the *entire* gift amount becomes taxable as "Income from Other Sources".
claims.note: Multiple sources confirm that if the aggregate value of gifts from non-relatives exceeds ₹50,000, the entire amount is taxable, not just the excess.

claims.claim: The taxability of gifts in India is primarily governed by Section 56(2)(x) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
claims.note: Section 56(2)(x) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, is consistently cited as the governing provision for gift taxation.

claims.claim: For an individual, "relative" is defined as: Spouse of the individual; Brother or sister of the individual; Brother or sister of the spouse of the individual; Brother or sister of either of the parents of the individual; Any lineal ascendant or descendant of the individual; Any lineal ascendant or descendant of the spouse of the individual; Spouse of any of the persons mentioned above.
claims.note: The definition of 'relative' provided in the article is consistent with the Income Tax Act, 1961, as detailed in various sources.

claims.claim: Gifts received on the occasion of marriage: Any gifts, whether cash or property, received by an individual at the time of their marriage are fully exempt from tax. This exemption applies only to the person getting married, not to other family members.
claims.note: Gifts received on the occasion of marriage are indeed fully exempt from tax for the recipient, regardless of the amount or donor.

claims.claim: Gifts received under a will or by way of inheritance: Property or money received through a will or as an inheritance is not subject to gift tax. This is because such transfers are typically covered under estate or inheritance laws, not income tax.
claims.note: Gifts received through a will or inheritance are exempt from income tax.

claims.claim: Is a gift from my employer taxable? Yes, gifts received from an employer exceeding ₹5,000 in a financial year are taxable as "perquisite" under the head "Salaries".
claims.note: As per the Income-tax Rules, 2026, the tax-free limit for non-cash gifts from an employer has been raised to ₹15,000 per financial year. Cash gifts from employers are always fully taxable, regardless of the amount.

claims.claim: If I give a gift, does the donor pay tax? Generally, the donor does not pay gift tax in India. The tax liability, if any, falls on the recipient of the gift, under Section 56(2)(x) of the Income Tax Act.
claims.note: The Gift Tax Act, 1958, was abolished in 1998. Currently, the tax liability on gifts falls on the recipient under Section 56(2)(x) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.

article_title: Diwali Gift Tax Rules 2026: Navigating the ₹50,000 Threshold
